pairs.rationale: The preceding appeal to desire greater gifts introduces love's priority even over speaking in human and angelic tongues. The present instruction pursues love and spiritual things, especially prophecy, carrying that priority into the discussion of speech.

Both describe tongue-speech directed to God when the congregation lacks understanding or interpretation. The later rule permits speaking to oneself and God while requiring silence in Church without an interpreter; this develops the distinction between divine address and human reception.

The stated human benefit of prophecy—building, encouragement and consolation—has a concrete comparison in Judas and Silas, explicitly called prophets, encouraging and strengthening the brothers with many words.

The contrast between building oneself and building the Church explains the later judgment that thanksgiving can be given well while another person is not built up. Both evaluate speech by its benefit beyond the speaker.

Both name prophecy, kinds of tongues and interpretation of tongues as distinct spiritual activities. The catalogue lists their distribution; this verse compares their congregational benefit and explicitly allows interpretation to affect that comparison.

Both list forms of congregational speech and test them by benefit or building up. Revelation, teaching and tongue-speech recur; the later gathering description also includes psalm and interpretation rather than reproducing this list exactly.

The flute-and-lyre question about recognizable notes supplies the analogy applied by the following 'So also with you': an intelligible word is needed for spoken communication to be known. The instruments are the illustration, not identifications of particular gifts.

Both connect a trumpet signal with war. Numbers gives an actual instruction for signaling against enemies; Paul uses the failure of an unclear trumpet to prepare people for battle as an illustration of intelligibility, without importing the whole military setting into worship.

The later preference for five words with the mind that instruct others provides a concrete application of the requirement for an intelligible word. It contrasts this teaching benefit with ten thousand words in a tongue.

The statement about many kinds of voices and none being voiceless is followed by the consequence introduced by 'Therefore': not knowing a voice's meaning makes speaker and hearer foreigners to each other. The source's voiceless wording is preserved.

The mutual foreignness caused by not knowing a voice's meaning develops the earlier warning that an unintelligible word is not known by the hearer. Foreigner here is the stated relation of incomprehension, not an identification of an ethnic group.

The earlier description gives each person's manifestation of the Spirit for the common benefit. The present instruction directs those zealous for spirits toward the Church's building up. The source's plural spirits wording remains distinct from the earlier singular Spirit.

The prayer that the tongue-speaker may interpret is related to the later practical requirement for an interpreter in congregational tongue-speech and silence when none is present. The texts do not promise that every such prayer immediately produces interpretation.

The next verse answers the problem of spirit praying while mind is unfruitful by resolving to pray and sing with both spirit and mind. This is the passage's own stated response, without defining an unmentioned physiological state.

The Psalm calls for music with understanding because God is King of all the earth. Paul likewise joins singing with the mind to singing with the spirit and applies the same pairing to prayer. This is a related worship instruction rather than an identified quotation.

Esdras blesses the Lord and the assembled people answer Amen. That intelligible corporate response provides a concrete comparison for Paul's question about how an uninitiated hearer could answer Amen to thanksgiving he does not understand.

The earlier contrast between self-building tongue-speech and Church-building prophecy explains why the other person's lack of building up matters even when the speaker gives thanks well. The goodness of thanksgiving and its intelligibility to others remain separate considerations.

Paul's thanksgiving for his own tongue-speaking corresponds to the closing instruction not to forbid speaking in tongues. This compares his positive treatment of the activity; the closing instruction does not independently establish the comparative amount of his speech.

Both concern instruction that the hearers understand. Nehemiah describes reading God's law with Esdras's knowledgeable explanation and the people's understanding; Paul prefers a few words with his mind that instruct others over a much larger amount in a tongue.

Both combine mature discernment with innocence concerning evil. Romans wants wisdom about good and innocence about evil; Corinthians calls for maturity in thinking and infancy in evil, distinguishing understanding from participation in wrongdoing.

The citation draws on Isaiah's other-tongue, lips and unheeding-people language. The supplied Isaiah says they will speak and that the people did not want to listen; Corinthians presents the Lord saying I will speak and they will not listen. The different wording is retained.

The sign conclusion follows the cited case of speech through other tongues to people who still do not listen. This preserves the argument's stated premise without defining every sign as a beneficial response or erasing the following example of an unbeliever exposed through prophecy.

Both describe adverse or perplexed reactions to a tongue-speaking gathering. Corinthians poses the outsiders' claim of madness; Acts reports perplexity and others mocking the speakers as full of sweet wine. Those are observers' reactions, not the narrator's endorsement or one identified event.

Exposure of an entering unbeliever through prophesying is compared with the Advocate's convicting the world. Corinthians assigns exposure and examination to the assembled speakers; John assigns conviction to the coming Advocate and names sin, righteousness and judgment.

Both portray outsiders acknowledging God's presence with the addressed people. Zechariah's men from the nations' languages grasp a Jewish man's garment and say God is with them; Corinthians's entering person falls down and worships after his heart's hidden things are revealed. The groups and settings remain distinct.

The meeting's varied contributions are all directed toward building up, corresponding to the earlier principle that each manifestation of the Spirit is given for common benefit. The present list supplies particular forms of participation.

Both regulate congregational speakers rather than permitting everyone to speak without limit. Tongue-speech is limited to two or at most three, in turn with interpretation; the prophetic rule has two or three speakers with others discerning. Their different reception duties are preserved.

The earlier distinction between speaking to God and human understanding explains the permitted address to oneself and God when there is no interpreter. Silence in Church here is conditional on that missing interpretation, not a ban on all tongue-speech.

Both combine reception of prophecy with discernment. Thessalonians says not to despise prophecies but to test all things and retain the good; Corinthians directs others to discern while two or three prophets speak.

The next explanation permits prophecy one by one for everyone's learning and encouragement. That purpose explains the instruction for the first speaker to become silent when another seated person receives a revelation.

Learning and encouragement through orderly prophecy apply the earlier description of prophecy as speech to people for building, encouragement and consolation. The connection is the stated human benefit, not an identification of particular prophets.

The assertion that prophets' spirits are subject to prophets grounds the adjacent instructions to yield the floor and speak one by one. The comparison follows the passage's own controlled turn-taking rather than supplying a theory of every spiritual experience.

Both ground communal life in the God of peace. The later closing joins encouragement, shared mind and peace with God's presence; this verse contrasts disorder with peace in the worship argument. The continuation about all Churches is retained in its original position.

Both direct women toward quietness and submission in a learning or Church setting. Corinthians speaks of silence and speaking in Churches; Timothy explicitly discusses learning, teaching and authority over a man. The scope descriptions remain as supplied rather than being made mechanically identical.

The earlier passage explicitly describes a woman praying or prophesying with a head-covering requirement, while this passage commands silence in Churches. This records the related internal contrast without deleting either statement or inventing an unstated harmonization.

The instruction to ask one's own husband at home supplies the stated learning arrangement alongside the immediately preceding Church-silence instruction. It does not itself identify a quoted legal verse or describe the household situation of every woman.

The rhetorical challenge to Corinthian exclusivity about God's word is related to Paul's earlier statement that his ways in Christ are taught everywhere in every Church. The connection is the wider setting of apostolic instruction, not a claim that all local circumstances are identical.

Both attribute the addressed apostolic instruction to the Lord's authority. Thessalonians names instructions given through the Lord Jesus; Corinthians requires a claimant to prophecy or spirituality to recognize the written instruction as the Lord's command.

The preceding recognition requirement supplies the object of this refusal to recognize. The actual passive result, he is not recognized, is preserved without replacing it with an imperative to remain ignorant or naming an unexpressed judging agent.

The conclusion repeats the opening priority of eagerly desiring prophecy and adds the express instruction not to forbid tongues. This is a summary of the chapter's qualified priorities, rather than a withdrawal of its interpretation and order requirements.

Both commend order in a Christian community. Corinthians commands that all be done fittingly and in order; Colossians describes Paul's joy at the recipients' order and firm faith, without repeating the particular speech procedures.

Both describe the recipients receiving the apostolic proclamation. Corinthians names the good news proclaimed and their standing in it; Thessalonians describes receiving the heard word as God's word, active among believers. The congregations and descriptions remain distinct.

Both attach an explicit continuation condition to receiving the gospel's benefit. Corinthians says to hold fast to the proclaimed word; Colossians says to continue founded and steadfast in faith without shifting from the gospel's hope.

Isaiah's sufferer is wounded for our iniquities and weakened for our sins. This supplies a specific scriptural suffering-for-others'-sins comparison for Paul's statement that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; Paul does not name one particular verse here.

Both place the Christ's resurrection on the third day within a written-scripture framework. Luke reports Jesus saying that it is written for the Christ to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day; Corinthians also explicitly includes burial.

Luke reports that the Lord has truly been raised and appeared to Simon, corresponding to the named appearance to Cephas, whose Simon alias is explicit in John1:42. Paul's further then-to-the-twelve statement is retained without replacing twelve with Luke's adjacent Eleven designation.

John explicitly identifies Simon as the one called Cephas, translated Peter. This supplies an actual alias warrant for the Cephas name in the appearance list; it concerns the name's identity, not a second narration of the resurrection appearance.

Both contrast believers remaining alive with those who have fallen asleep. Corinthians gives the present survival status of the appearance-witness group; Thessalonians discusses the living and sleeping at the Lord's coming. It does not independently attest five hundred witnesses or identify those two groups.

Both describe the risen Jesus appearing to apostles. Acts names His chosen apostles and His presenting Himself alive after suffering over forty days. It does not name this James or establish the exact membership of Paul's all-the-apostles group.

Paul's defense speech reports Jesus saying that He appeared to him to appoint him a servant and witness. This provides a particular comparison for Paul's claimed appearance; the untimely-born image and last position belong to the Corinthian list, not the Acts statement.

Both are Paul's own acknowledgment that he persecuted God's Church. Galatians describes its severity and ravaging; Corinthians makes that past conduct the stated reason for calling himself unworthy of apostleship.

Both credit Paul's apostolic work to divine action rather than himself alone. Corinthians names God's grace with him in his abundant labor; Romans restricts his account to what Christ worked through him for Gentile obedience in word and deed.

The declaration of a common proclamation by Paul or the others refers back to the handed-over message of Christ's death for sins, burial and third-day resurrection. This is an internal summary of the stated gospel content, not an identification of every preacher.

Both report the proposition that there is no resurrection. Corinthians attributes it to some among the recipients; Acts attributes it to Sadducees and adds denials concerning angel and spirit. The Corinthian people are not identified as Sadducees or assigned every additional denial.

The later conditional repeats this argument: denying the raising of the dead would also exclude Christ's having been raised. These are hypothetical consequences within Paul's rebuttal, not his assertion that Christ remained dead.

Both draw futility of faith from the same if-Christ-has-not-been-raised premise. The present verse also calls the proclamation empty; the later verse adds remaining in sins. The conditional premise is preserved.

The hypothetical charge of false witness depends on the testimony that God raised Christ. Acts gives Peter's positive statement that God raised Jesus and that they are witnesses. The positive testimony is compared with the consequence of denying it, without declaring Paul actually a false witness.

This restates the earlier link between denial of resurrection of the dead and denial of Christ's resurrection. Its repeated conditional premise belongs to the same argument and is not an independent report that Christ was not raised.

Corinthians presents the negative consequence of Christ not being raised: futile faith and remaining in sins. Romans positively connects His being handed over with trespasses and His being raised with justification. The two forms connect resurrection with the believers' condition before God.

The counterfactual loss of those asleep in Christ is contrasted with the positive hope for those who have fallen asleep because Jesus died and rose. Thessalonians explicitly addresses grief and God's bringing them with Jesus.

Paul's counterfactual restriction of hope to this life is compared with Peter's living hope through Jesus Christ's resurrection and an imperishable inheritance kept in heaven. Future hope beyond present life is the connection, not an identical formulation about pity.

Both give Christ primacy in relation to the dead: firstfruits of those asleep here, firstborn from the dead with first place in all things there. The firstfruits and firstborn images remain distinct rather than becoming interchangeable wording.
Both state that death came through a human being. Romans relates death's entry to sin through one person; Corinthians pairs that death-through-a-human claim with resurrection through a human being.

Both contrast the effects of one person with those of the One bringing life. Corinthians names Adam and Christ and dying and being made alive; Romans contrasts trespass and righteous act, disobedience and obedience, condemnation and justification of life. Their actual all and many formulations are retained.

Both describe an order involving believers at the Lord's coming. Corinthians places Christ the firstfruits before those belonging to Him; Thessalonians places the dead in Christ rising before the living are caught up with them. These are different stated comparisons of order, not identical uses of first.

Both place Christ over rule, authority and power. Ephesians describes His resurrection, enthronement and all things subjected under His feet; Corinthians describes bringing those powers to nothing and handing the kingdom to God the Father. Ephesians does not repeat that final handover.

The Psalm's enthronement at the Lord's right hand until enemies become a footstool corresponds to Christ's reign until all enemies are under His feet. The enthronement, until and enemy-underfoot pattern is shared while the original pronouns are left as supplied.

Both describe death being brought to nothing or abolished in relation to Christ's saving work. Corinthians places death last in the enemy sequence; Timothy describes the Savior's appearing, abolishing death and bringing life and incorruptibility to light through the gospel. The temporal formulations remain distinct.

The all-things-under-feet saying corresponds to the Psalm's appointment over God's handiwork and subjection of everything beneath the human figure's feet. Paul applies the saying in his Christ argument and explicitly excludes the One doing the subjecting from the all being subjected.

The Son's subjection and God being all in all complete the end-directed movement already described as handing the kingdom to God the Father. This follows the letter's own sequence and preserves its distinct Son and God roles without adding an unprinted explanation of divine nature.

The repeated if-the-dead-are-not-raised premise joins the question about baptism for the dead to the preceding consequences for Christ's resurrection and faith. The link is the argument's conditional logic; it does not define the custom's participants, procedure or efficacy.

Paul's catalogue of frequent journey dangers supplies concrete comparisons for his question about constant danger. Rivers, robbers, peoples, cities, wilderness, sea and false brothers are named there; no one event is made an hourly incident log.

Both express Paul's ongoing exposure to death in relation to Jesus. Corinthians's daily-dying language is compared with always carrying Jesus' dying in the body and being handed over to death for His sake; this is not a claim of repeated literal deaths and resurrections.

The eat-and-drink-for-tomorrow-we-die saying occurs in Isaiah amid feasting in place of the requested mourning. Paul uses it as the consequence of the no-resurrection premise. The quotation does not identify his separate Ephesus beast-fighting statement with a narrated riot or arena episode.

Both warn that harmful companionship changes conduct. Proverbs specifically warns against an angry companion lest one learn his ways and acquire snares; Corinthians gives the broader bad-company/good-habits maxim. This is a thematic comparison, not a claim that Proverbs supplies the maxim verbatim.

Both call for ethical sobriety rather than sleeping or losing moral awareness. Thessalonians develops watchfulness, day and night and salvation's hope; Corinthians commands sobering up, avoiding sin and addressing lack of knowledge of God. No medical condition is inferred.

The later sown-and-raised contrasts answer the question about the resurrection body through corruption and incorruption, dishonor and glory, weakness and power, natural and spiritual body. These are the passage's descriptions, not a supplied mechanical account of resurrection.

Both use a grain's dying as the image for ensuing life or fruitfulness. John applies the falling grain to the Son of Man's approaching glorification; Corinthians uses sowing and being made alive in the resurrection-body argument. The image's applications remain distinct.

The contrast between the bare grain sown and the body that will come is followed by God's giving each seed its own body as He wished. The next verse supplies the stated divine action behind this seed-and-body illustration.

Both connect God with the diverse forms arising through seed. Genesis describes God's command and vegetation and fruit trees with seed according to kind; Paul says God gives each seed its own body. The passages' kind and body terms are not turned into a modern taxonomy.

The creation account distinguishes water creatures, birds, land animals and human beings, the categories Paul names in describing different flesh. Genesis supplies a concrete creation comparison; it does not state Paul's subsequent resurrection-body conclusions.

The following distinctions among the glory of sun, moon and stars provide particular heavenly examples after the general distinction between heavenly and earthly bodies and their glory. The passage does not assign a named resurrected person's rank to a particular celestial object.

Both distinguish heavenly lights and stars. Genesis names the greater and lesser lights with their day and night functions and the stars; Paul names sun, moon and stars and their differing glory. Their role and glory descriptions are related without being treated as identical wording.

Both look toward release from corruption involving God's people and bodily redemption. Romans describes creation's freedom from slavery to corruption and believers awaiting redemption of the body; Corinthians describes the body's sowing in corruption and raising in incorruption.

Both describe bodily transformation toward glory through divine power. Philippians speaks of the body of humiliation conformed to Christ's glorious body by His working; Corinthians contrasts dishonor with glory and weakness with power.

The natural-body/spiritual-body contrast is followed by the stated sequence of natural first and spiritual afterward. The explanation remains a sequence within the same body argument, without replacing the actual body language with disembodied existence.

The statement that the first human became a living soul quotes Genesis's account of the man formed from dust and receiving the breath of life. Paul's last-Adam/life-giving-spirit contrast is his additional statement, not an inserted clause in Genesis.

The preceding first-human/last-Adam comparison supplies the immediate basis for the natural-first/spiritual-afterward sequence. The living-soul and life-giving-spirit descriptions remain distinct in that argument.

The first human's earthly, dust-derived origin corresponds directly to God's forming the man from the earth's dust in Genesis. This target supplies the first half of the comparison, rather than an explicit Genesis account of the second human from heaven.

Jesus explicitly says He came down from heaven to do the Sender's will. That provides a particular comparison for the second human's heavenly origin; it does not add the omitted Lord title or a description of the body's material construction to Corinthians.

The next verse applies the dusty/heavenly likeness pattern to the addressed we: bearing the dusty one's image and subsequently the heavenly One's image. This is the letter's own application of resemblance between the head figure and those associated with him.

Both describe believers' conformity to the Son or heavenly One through image language. Romans says they were predestined to be conformed to the Son's image; Corinthians sets future bearing of the heavenly image against the already-borne dusty image.

Both connect entry or inheritance of God's kingdom with a distinction involving flesh and a divinely given transformation. John speaks of birth from water and Spirit and flesh-born versus Spirit-born; Corinthians speaks of corruption and incorruption in the resurrection argument. These are different applications, not identical procedures.

Both distinguish believers who remain alive from those who have fallen asleep in the setting of the Lord's coming. Corinthians explicitly says all will be changed despite not all sleeping; Thessalonians explicitly describes the dead rising and the living being caught up, without using the all-will-be-changed formula.

Both join a trumpet with the raising of the dead. Corinthians calls it the last trumpet and specifies incorruptibility and change; Thessalonians calls it God's trumpet with the Lord's descent and the dead in Christ rising first. Their different labels are retained.

Both picture overcoming mortality through clothing imagery. Corinthians says the corruptible and mortal must put on incorruption and immortality; the other letter desires being clothed over so mortality is swallowed by life, rather than being found permanently unclothed.

The distinctive death-and-swallowing language supplies the scriptural correspondence, with a material wording contrast. The pinned Isaiah says Death swallowed, having prevailed; Corinthians says Death has been swallowed up in victory. Isaiah's active swallower is not normalized into Paul's passive formulation.

Both address death-related powers with where-is-your questions. The actual Hosea asks Death about punishment and Hades about sting; Corinthians asks death about victory and sting. The altered term and second addressee are preserved instead of making the two English passages identical.

Both connect sin, law or commandment, and death. Romans describes sin taking opportunity through the commandment, deceiving and killing; Corinthians calls sin death's sting and law sin's power. Romans's adjacent declaration that the law is holy prevents equating law itself with sin.

Both credit God's gift through Jesus Christ in contrast with sin and death. Romans names sin's wages as death and God's gift as eternal life in Christ Jesus; Corinthians thanks God for victory through the Lord Jesus Christ.

The earlier assurance of each worker receiving wages according to labor supplies a specific internal comparison for labor not being empty in the Lord. The call to steadfast, abundant work rests in this chapter's resurrection-and-victory conclusion, not a calculated payment schedule.
